summaries.title: Chief Economist's Weekly Watch – March 9, 2026: Geopolitical Tensions, Inflation Watch, & Labor Demand Signals
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Trepp discusses current market conditions and key economic indicators as of March 9, 2026. It highlights three primary areas to monitor: geopolitical tensions and oil prices, inflation metrics, and labor demand signals.

The report describes how escalating tensions in the Middle East have led to rising oil prices, which could significantly impact commercial real estate (CRE) markets. Increased energy costs could affect construction and transportation expenses, putting pressure on development feasibility, especially in the lodging sector, where they might correlate with increased air travel and reduced discretionary travel demand.

It notes that the upcoming Consumer Price Index (CPI) report on Wednesday and the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) report on Friday will provide insights into inflation trends. Rising oil prices may complicate the narrative of easing inflation if they subsequently lead to broader price increases. Additionally, the preliminary consumer sentiment report will be crucial to track, particularly regarding inflation expectations that can influence rate forecasts and commercial real estate borrowing costs.

The report also emphasizes the importance of the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) in assessing labor demand. A decline in job openings, as suggested by recent job reports, may support the Federal Reserve's potential for mid-year interest rate cuts, which could lower Treasury yields. A sustained decrease in openings related to office sectors could exacerbate leasing challenges and increase the risk of subleasing, negatively impacting asset valuations and refinancing prospects for properties already experiencing high vacancy rates.

Overall, these factors will significantly inform market interpretations regarding inflation, labor demand, and interest rates, which are pivotal for CRE financing conditions.

Source URL: https://www.trepp.com/trepptalk/chief-economists-weekly-watch-march-9-2026
summaries.headline: Escalating Geopolitical Tensions and Inflation Trends Impacting Commercial Real Estate Markets: A March 2026 Overview
summaries.blurb: In its March 2026 overview, Trepp examines how escalating geopolitical tensions and rising oil prices are reshaping the commercial real estate landscape. With inflation metrics on the horizon and labor demand signals shifting, the report reveals potential challenges for development, especially in the lodging sector. Dive into the essential economic indicators that could influence market dynamics and financing conditions in the coming months.

summaries.title: ABC’s Construction Backlog Indicator Rebounds in February, Contractor Confidence Grows
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Associated Builders and Contractors indicates that its Construction Backlog Indicator rose to 8.1 months in February, reflecting a 0.1 month increase from January but a 0.2 month decrease from February 2025. This data comes from an ABC member survey conducted from February 20 to March 6.

The report highlights a sharp increase in backlog for the Middle States, which includes states like Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio, marking it as the only region with higher backlog than one year ago. Furthermore, ABC’s Construction Confidence Index showed improvements in sales and staffing expectations for February, although profit margin expectations declined. All three components remain above the growth threshold of 50.

ABC Chief Economist Anirban Basu noted that while backlog has rebounded from a four-year low in January, it is still low by historical standards, emphasizing the Midwestern region's unexpected economic growth post-pandemic. He mentioned that contractors engaged in data center projects have longer backlogs (11.2 months) compared to those in other sectors (7.6 months). However, the ongoing conflict in Iran may impact demand for certain construction types due to rising materials prices and borrowing costs.

Basu expressed cautious optimism regarding profit margins over the next six months, but raised concerns about potential challenges stemming from rising oil prices which could affect hiring expectations that had recently improved, reaching their highest level since March 2025.

Source URL: https://www.abc.org/News-Media/News-Releases/abcs-construction-backlog-indicator-rebounds-in-february-contractor-confidence-grows
summaries.headline: February Sees Uptick in Construction Backlog and Contractor Confidence, But Profit Margins Remain a Concern
summaries.blurb: February brought a noteworthy rebound in construction backlog and contractor confidence, with the Associated Builders and Contractors reporting an increase to 8.1 months. While the Middle States showed remarkable growth, concerns linger over declining profit margins amidst rising material costs. ABC’s Chief Economist Anirban Basu offers cautious optimism for the coming months, underscoring the mixed signals in today's construction landscape.

summaries.title: Nonresidential Construction Spending Plunges in December, Says ABC
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from ABC reveals that national nonresidential construction spending experienced a decrease of 0.6% in December, based on an analysis of data from the U.S. Census Bureau. The seasonally adjusted annualized spending level for nonresidential construction reached $1.24 trillion.

The report indicates that spending fell in 12 of the 16 nonresidential subcategories on a monthly basis. Specifically, private nonresidential spending declined by 0.7%, while public nonresidential construction spending saw a decrease of 0.4% during the same period.

ABC Chief Economist Anirban Basu commented on the trends, stating, “Nonresidential construction spending contracted sharply in December.” He noted that this downturn was particularly pronounced in the manufacturing sector, which has seen a nearly 16% decrease since its peak in August 2024. Basu attributed the ongoing decline in manufacturing-related spending to factors such as trade policy uncertainty and the diminishing impacts of the CHIPS Act, predicting that this trend would likely persist over the next several quarters.

Basu further explained that although manufacturing is a key contributor to the nonresidential construction decline, it is not the only factor. He pointed out that eight of the 11 private nonresidential subsegments experienced contractions in December, leading to a total decline in private nonresidential spending of 1.8% year over year. In light of these trends, Basu remarked that it was predictable for ABC’s Construction Backlog Indicator to drop to a four-year low in January.

Source URL: https://www.abc.org/News-Media/News-Releases/nonresidential-construction-spending-plunges-in-december-says-abc
summaries.headline: Nonresidential Construction Spending Falls 0.6% in December Amid Broad Sector Declines, Warns ABC
summaries.blurb: In a striking December report, ABC reveals a 0.6% decline in national nonresidential construction spending, reaching an annualized level of $1.24 trillion. The downturn, driven by significant drops in the manufacturing sector and various private nonresidential subcategories, signals ongoing challenges influenced by trade policy uncertainty and the waning effects of the CHIPS Act. With spending contracting sharply, experts project that the slowdown could continue well into the coming quarters.

summaries.title: ABC: Construction Materials Prices Surge in January, Driven Again by Tariffs
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) indicates that construction input prices rose by 0.7% in January compared to the prior month, with nonresidential construction input prices increasing by 0.6%. Year-over-year, overall construction input prices are up 2.3%, while nonresidential construction input prices have increased by 2.9%.

The report notes that prices rose in two out of three energy categories, with crude petroleum prices increasing by 1.8% and unprocessed energy materials by 0.4%; however, natural gas prices fell by 2.9% in January. ABC Chief Economist Anirban Basu highlighted that nonresidential construction input prices surged at an annualized rate of 7.1% in January, largely due to significant increases in tarifficated products such as copper wire and cable, iron and steel, and industrial controls equipment.

Despite these fluctuations, Basu stated that concerns about overall input price escalation are minimal, with nonresidential materials prices only up 2.9% over the past year and nearly flat since September. He remarked that while trade policy may continue to exert upward pressure on specific input prices, particularly those affected by the Section 232 tariffs, price increases are expected to remain moderate as long as energy prices are stable and demand is subdued. Contractor sentiment regarding profit margins showed improvement in January as per ABC's Construction Confidence Index, although it is still below the levels from the previous year.

Source URL: https://www.abc.org/News-Media/News-Releases/abc-construction-materials-prices-surge-in-january-driven-again-by-tariffs
summaries.headline: Construction Input Prices Rise 0.7% in January, Driven by Tariffs and Energy Trends
summaries.blurb: In a revealing February report from Associated Builders and Contractors, construction input prices saw a 0.7% bump in January, primarily influenced by tariffs on key materials like copper and steel. While nonresidential construction input prices climbed by 0.6%, the annual increase stands at 2.9%, reflecting a cautious optimism in contractor profitability. Despite the fluctuations in energy categories, experts predict that moderate price increases will prevail as demand remains steady and energy prices stabilize.

summaries.title: ABC: All But 5 States Had Construction Unemployment Rates Below 8% in December 2025
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from ABC indicated that the national construction unemployment rate in December 2025 was 5.0%, marking a 0.2% decrease from December 2024. The analysis, based on U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data, revealed that 60% of states (30 states) had lower construction unemployment rates compared to the previous year, while 17 states experienced higher rates, and three states maintained the same rates (New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Texas). Notably, only five states reported construction unemployment rates above 8%.

Due to the 2025 government shutdown, October labor data were not collected, resulting in unavailable data. The non-seasonally adjusted construction employment payroll saw an increase of 12,000 compared to December 2024, the smallest year-over-year increase since March 2021. Seasonally adjusted payroll construction employment reached 8.3 million, surpassing the pre-pandemic peak of 7.6 million by 9.1%.

In December 2025, 30 states had lower construction unemployment rates than in December 2019, while 18 states had higher and two states (Georgia and New Mexico) maintained the same rate. Bernard Markstein, president and chief economist of Markstein Advisors, noted several challenges for the industry, including increased building material prices and a shortage of skilled workers due to immigration enforcement, but also highlighted a potential benefit from a more accommodating Federal Reserve policy leading to lower interest rates.

In December, the national construction unemployment rate rose by 0.9% from November. Among the states, Alabama, Montana, and New Mexico saw lower rates, while 44 states reported increases.

The states with the lowest construction unemployment rates for December were:

- Hawaii: 2.0%
- Oklahoma: 2.5%
- Colorado: 2.7%
- Georgia, Indiana, Mississippi (tie): 2.8%

Hawaii and Indiana achieved their record lowest December unemployment rates, and Colorado had its second-lowest.

Conversely, the highest estimated construction unemployment rates were in:

- Illinois: 9.4%
- New Jersey: 10.1%
- Connecticut: 10.5%
- Rhode Island: 11.2%
- Minnesota: 13.4%

Rhode Island did record its lowest rate since December 2022. 

Source URL: https://www.abc.org/News-Media/News-Releases/abc-all-but-5-states-had-construction-unemployment-rates-below-8-in-december-2025
summaries.headline: February Report: National Construction Unemployment Drops to 5% as 30 States See Improvement in Rates
summaries.blurb: The latest February report from ABC reveals a promising shift in the construction industry, with national unemployment dropping to 5% in December 2025, a 0.2% decrease from the previous year. Notably, 30 states saw lower construction unemployment rates, highlighting a resilient sector despite challenges like rising material prices and skilled labor shortages. As the industry navigates these hurdles, the potential for continued growth is on the horizon.

summaries.title: ADP National Employment Report February 2026
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from ADP reveals that private sector employment increased by 63,000 jobs in February 2026, with annual pay rising 4.5% year-over-year. The report, produced in collaboration with the Stanford Digital Economy Lab, analyzes anonymized weekly payroll data from over 26 million private-sector employees in the U.S. Dr. Nela Richardson, ADP's chief economist, noted, “We've seen an increase in hiring and pay gains remain solid, especially for job-stayers,” though hiring was concentrated in a few sectors, leading to a record low pay premium for changing jobs.

In detail, the report highlights:

**Jobs Report:**
- Private employers added 63,000 jobs in February, marking the best job gains since July 2025.
- Growth was particularly strong in the construction and education/health services sectors.
- Breakdown by industry:
  - Goods-producing added 16,000 jobs.
  - Service-providing added 47,000 jobs, with notable contributions from education/health services (58,000 jobs) and information (11,000 jobs).
- Regional changes indicated the South gained the most jobs (37,000), while the Midwest lost 4,000.
- Job creation varied by establishment size, with small establishments adding 60,000 jobs.

**Pay Insights:**
- Pay for job-stayers increased by 4.5% year-over-year, remaining stable from the previous month.
- For job-changers, annualized pay growth slowed to 6.3%.
- Pay growth varied by industry and firm size, with small firms showing the lowest growth rates.

The report also revised January's employment figures, lowering the number of jobs added from 22,000 to 11,000. The next ADP National Employment Report is scheduled for release on April 1, 2026.

Source URL: https://adp-ri-nrip-static.adp.com/artifacts/us_ner/20260304/ADP_NATIONAL_EMPLOYMENT_REPORT_Press_Release_2026_02%20FINAL.pdf
summaries.headline: Private Sector Jobs Rise by 63,000 in February; Pay Gains Solid at 4.5%
summaries.blurb: February brought a promising surge in private sector jobs, with an increase of 63,000 positions according to the latest ADP report. Annual pay gains remain robust at 4.5%, particularly benefiting those who stay with their employers—though job-changers may be feeling the sting of a slowing pay growth trend. As hiring focuses on sectors like construction and education, the employment landscape showcases both opportunities and challenges ahead.

summaries.title: The Slow Climb: How Tariffs Gradually Raised Retail Prices in 2025
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from the Federal Reserve titled "The Slow Climb: How Tariffs Gradually Raised Retail Prices in 2025" examines the gradual impact of tariffs on consumer prices using comprehensive retail spending data. The study finds that price pressures from tariffs emerged incrementally rather than as abrupt spikes. Specifically, goods imported from China saw an 8.5% price increase year-over-year by December 2025, with a documented tariff pass-through rate to consumers of at least 30%.

The analysis employs a methodology that combines item-level retail spending data from 200,000 U.S. households with details about product origins. This approach leads to the construction of a Fisher Price Index (FPI) that closely matches the Official PCE deflator for food, underscoring the reliability of the dataset. Gross expenditures dominated by grocery purchases accounted for 44.1% of spending among the tracked categories.

Using the dataset, the report identifies imported goods' price changes, noting that Chinese goods experienced the most significant increases compared to imports from other countries. Before April 2025, year-over-year inflation for imported goods hovered around zero; however, after tariff announcements, prices for Chinese imports climbed markedly. By December, year-over-year inflation for such goods reached over 8%.

The report integrates various figures that illustrate these findings, including capping tariffs' impact on consumer prices and providing evidence of a continued price increase pattern post-announcement. Key results suggest that retailers continue to absorb costs, potentially delaying further price adjustments in response to tariff environments.

Overall, the findings highlight a consistent trend of rising prices due to tariffs, refuting the notion of a one-time spike and underscoring a gradual adjustment in retail pricing strategies throughout 2025.

Source URL: https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/the-slow-climb-how-tariffs-gradually-raised-retail-prices-in-2025-20260305.html
summaries.headline: "Federal Reserve Report Reveals Gradual Price Increases from Tariffs Amid Retail Spending Trends in 2025"
summaries.blurb: In its latest report, the Federal Reserve unveils the nuanced effects of tariffs on consumer pricing throughout 2025, revealing that price increases were incremental rather than sudden. Highlighting an 8.5% rise in prices for goods imported from China by December, the study combines extensive household spending data to present a clearer picture of how tariffs reshaped retail landscapes. This comprehensive analysis challenges the perception of immediate price shocks, illustrating a gradual shift in consumer spending dynamics.

summaries.title: Beige Book - March 4, 2026
summaries.summaryText:
A March 4, 2026, report from the Federal Reserve, titled Beige Book, provides a summary of economic conditions across the twelve Federal Reserve Districts.

Overall economic activity increased at a slight to moderate pace in seven Districts, while five reported flat or declining activity. Consumer spending saw a slight increase, but two Districts noted ongoing declines affected by economic uncertainty. Retail traffic slowed in areas impacted by winter storms, and some urban regions experienced reduced demand due to immigration enforcement. Auto sales generally declined, attributed to affordability issues. Manufacturing improved with eight Districts reporting growth and two declining, while many noted increases in new orders. Transportation activity was mixed, with three Districts contracting and two experiencing modest growth. Financial services remained stable, primarily driven by commercial lending. Residential real estate and construction saw slight declines, hindered by low inventories, whereas nonresidential construction increased modestly. Agricultural conditions were flat, and energy sector activity showed modest growth. Most Districts maintained optimism about future economic growth.

In labor markets, employment levels were stable, with seven Districts not reporting hiring changes. Some firms cited rising nonlabor input costs and demand uncertainty as reasons for flat or decreasing employment. Companies in various sectors explored automation for efficiency, focusing on productivity rather than worker replacement. Wage growth was modest, particularly for skilled trades, and upward pressure on total compensation persisted due to rising health insurance premiums.

Price increases were moderate, with eight Districts reporting moderate growth and four noting slight increases. Costs rose for various nonlabor inputs, and tariffs contributed to higher costs in nine Districts. While some firms passed on tariff-related costs to customers, many held prices stable amid increasing price sensitivity. Overall, firms anticipated a slower pace of price increases in the near term.

Highlights by individual Districts include:

- **Boston:** Flat economic activity, slight decline in employment, and modest price rises amid tariff pressures.
- **New York:** Modest economic decline, flat employment, and steady wage growth, with slight consumer spending increase.
- **Philadelphia:** Modest economic growth despite adverse weather, with increased sales activity and modest inflation.
- **Cleveland:** Modest increases in business activity, particularly in manufacturing and construction, with robust nonlabor cost pressures.
- **Richmond:** Modest growth, flat retail spending, and increased commercial real estate activity.
- **Atlanta:** Modest to moderate economic expansion, with improved housing demand and mixed transportation activity.
- **Chicago:** Slight economic increase, with modest rises in manufacturing, consumer spending, and wages.
- **St. Louis:** Unchanged economic activity expected to grow in the coming months, with moderate price and wage increases.
- **Minneapolis:** Slight decline in economic activity, softened employment, and moderate wage growth.
- **Kansas City:** Slight economic increase, stable labor conditions, and modest price increases.
- **Dallas:** Moderate expansion, particularly in manufacturing, with slight growth in employment and prices.
- **San Francisco:** Slight contraction in economic activity, with stable employment but layoffs in technology services.

This report was prepared at the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland based on information collected on or before February 23, 2026. 

Source URL: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/beigebook202602-summary.htm
summaries.headline: Federal Reserve Beige Book: Mixed Economic Activity Across Districts Amid Modest Growth and Ongoing Uncertainty
summaries.blurb: The latest Federal Reserve Beige Book reveals a tapestry of economic conditions across the twelve Districts, highlighting both modest growth and notable declines. While consumer spending shows a slight uptick, challenges from winter storms and immigration enforcement have dampened retail traffic in key areas. With mixed results in manufacturing and modest optimism about future growth, this report captures the nuanced landscape of America’s economy as it navigates ongoing uncertainties.

summaries.title: FOMC Minutes - January 2026 Meeting
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from the Federal Reserve outlines the minutes from the January 2026 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), held on January 27 and 28, 2026. The meeting included the election of members and alternate members of the FOMC, with key officers selected to serve until 2027. Specifically, Jerome H. Powell was appointed Chair, and John C. Williams was appointed Vice Chair.

Market developments were discussed, showing an upbeat outlook for economic resilience, with forecasts rising for GDP growth. While inflation and unemployment expectations remained stable, market indicators suggested potential rate cuts later in the year, indicating expectations for two 25 basis point cuts in the federal funds rate.

The report provided insights into Treasury market developments, noting stable short-term yields and slightly increased longer-term yields. Inflation compensation in these markets dropped as consumer price index readings lowered, attributed to reduced energy prices and tariff pass-throughs. Discussions included fluctuations in equity prices, with a notable focus on the underperformance of large technology firms.

Internationally, expectations for dollar depreciation were observed alongside differing predictions for economic growth compared to other economies. Reports indicated a significant depreciation of the dollar linked to inquiries from the Federal Reserve about the dollar-yen exchange rate.

In money markets, the effective federal funds rate was stable, aided by an increase in liquidity. Also, conditions in short-term funding markets remained stable, with ongoing repo operations leading to lower-than-expected pressures during year-end.

The economic outlook indicated real GDP growth was expected to be above potential growth through 2028 due to easing tariff impacts. Labor market conditions stabilized but showed mixed signals in job gains. Consumer price inflation was noted to be elevated, with ongoing uncertainty regarding its trajectory.

Participants in the meeting expressed concerns about high asset valuations and vulnerabilities associated with debt levels, particularly relating to rising risks in the private credit market and potential systemic risks tied to hedge funds. The Federal Reserve’s staff projected a stronger economic activity in comparison to the previous month's assessments, noting that inflation expectations had moderated amid technological advancements potentially benefiting productivity.

In terms of monetary policy, while most members agreed to maintain the current target range for the federal funds rate, there were discussions about the need for potential adjustments based on future economic indicators. The consensus reflected a commitment to balancing employment support with keeping inflation in check at 2 percent, while acknowledging various risks surrounding the economic environment.

The Committee voted to instruct the Federal Reserve Bank of New York to conduct transactions to maintain a federal funds rate target range and to execute operations as necessary, including the management of investment purchases.

The next meeting of the Committee was scheduled for March 17-18, 2026.

Source URL: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20260128.htm
summaries.headline: FOMC Minutes Reveal Economic Optimism Amid Calls for Rate Cuts and Rising Risks
summaries.blurb: The latest FOMC minutes reveal a cautiously optimistic economic outlook, with projected GDP growth hinting at potential rate cuts later in the year. Amidst stable inflation and employment expectations, discussions highlighted concerns about high asset valuations and risks in private credit markets. These insights set the stage for the Federal Reserve's upcoming meetings as they navigate the balance between fostering growth and controlling inflation.

summaries.title: How Will the Iran Conflict Impact Oil Prices?
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Goldman Sachs details the impacts of escalating conflicts in Iran on oil prices. Following US and Israeli military actions, oil prices surged, influenced significantly by potential transit disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounts for approximately one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies.

Goldman Sachs strategists indicate a risk premium of about $14 per barrel, reflecting increased trader demands following the conflict. The report outlines estimates suggesting that a full month of blocked flows could lead to price increases of $15 per barrel without offsets, with various scenarios providing lower estimates depending on the utilization of spare pipeline capacities and strategic reserve releases.

Historical patterns indicate temporary spikes in oil prices can follow geopolitical events; for example, during mid-2022, oil prices exceeded estimated fair value to a significant extent due to similar uncertainties. In 2025, Iran produced approximately 3.5 million barrels per day (mb/d) of crude, contributing about 4% to global supplies, and faced ongoing export levels of 1.7 mb/d for crude and condensates.

The report warns that LNG prices could significantly rise if transit through the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted, with estimates suggesting European gas prices might reach approximately 74 EUR/MWh if LNG flows are fully halted for a month, and over 100 EUR/MWh in cases of longer disruptions. 

This article serves an educational purpose, and Goldman Sachs disclaims any obligations regarding its accuracy or liability. 

Source URL: https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/how-will-the-iran-conflict-impact-oil-prices
summaries.headline: Goldman Sachs Report: Iran Conflict Fuels Oil Prices Surge, Risks Near $15 Increase Per Barrel
summaries.blurb: Goldman Sachs' latest report reveals that escalating conflicts in Iran could drive oil prices up by as much as $15 per barrel, as disruptions in the crucial Strait of Hormuz loom large. With a risk premium of around $14 per barrel already in play, the report highlights the potential for significant price volatility and its impact on global energy markets. As tensions rise, traders are keeping a keen eye on these developments, sensing major ramifications for both oil and LNG prices.

summaries.title: Forecasts for the World’s Biggest Economies in 2026
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from Goldman Sachs Research outlines forecasts for global economies in 2026, predicting a global real GDP growth of 2.9%, surpassing the consensus estimate of 2.7%. The US economy is projected to grow by 2.8%, driven by tax cuts from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and easing inflation, which is expected to decrease to 2.2% by December 2026. 

For the euro area, GDP growth is forecasted at 1.3%, supported by increased fiscal spending in Germany and robust growth in Spain at 2.4%. However, challenges with energy prices and export competition from China persist. 

Mainland China is expected to see a 4.8% GDP growth, attributed to rising exports and an increasing current account surplus projected at 4.1%. 

Japan's growth forecast is at 0.6%, driven by domestic demand and private consumption increasing by 0.9%. The Bank of Japan is anticipated to implement more frequent interest rate hikes starting in July 2026. 

In the UK, a mixed outlook predicts 1.5% GDP growth, with a rise in unemployment anticipated in early 2026, although cooling inflation may lead to interest rate cuts by the Bank of England. 

This report emphasizes specific economic conditions and projections for major global economies without providing recommendations or financial advice. 

Source URL: https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/forecasts-for-the-worlds-biggest-economies-in-2026
summaries.headline: Goldman Sachs Forecasts Global GDP Growth of 2.9% in 2026, Led by Strong US and China Economies.
summaries.blurb: Goldman Sachs' latest report projects a robust global GDP growth of 2.9% for 2026, outpacing the consensus estimate. The United States is expected to lead with a 2.8% growth fueled by new tax cuts and easing inflation, while Mainland China's impressive forecast of 4.8% growth reflects rising exports and a strengthening current account surplus. As economic landscapes evolve, insights from this report provide a compelling glimpse into the trajectories of the world's major economies.

summaries.title: Why Has Productivity in the US Construction Industry Stagnated?
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from Goldman Sachs explores the stagnation of productivity in the US construction industry, indicating that it has been declining at an average rate of 0.6% per year since 1965, contrasting with the wider economy's growth of about 1.6%. Elsie Peng, an economist at Goldman Sachs Research, attributes this underperformance to a lack of innovation, increased regulation, and mismeasurement issues.

The report notes that major construction machinery has not significantly advanced since the 1950s, leading to underwhelming innovations in the sector. The share of industrial machines in construction costs rose sharply until the 1970s but has since plateaued. Additionally, pre-fabrication technology, once pivotal in housing production, has dwindled from one-third of new residential units to just 5%. 

Peng emphasizes that while other industries have benefitted from technological advances, construction has not seen similar spillover effects. This results in relatively low productivity growth linked to innovation. The report quantifies the potential impact of increased innovation intensity, estimating that a 1% rise could enhance productivity growth by 0.2 percentage points annually.

Another significant factor is the impact of housing regulation, which has a negative effect on productivity growth, with the report estimating that a 1% rise in regulatory intensity can reduce productivity growth by 0.6 percentage points. Delays from strict approval processes and restrictions on building size contribute to these challenges, limiting competition and increasing development barriers. 

The report also addresses issues of mismeasurement in construction output, suggesting that the failure to account for quality improvements and the inappropriate use of residential price indices may create a downward bias in productivity metrics. If corrected, this could portray a more favorable average annual labor productivity growth of -0.3% instead of -1.0% from 1990 to 2024.

Source URL: https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/why-has-productivity-in-the-us-construction-industry-stagnated
summaries.headline: Goldman Sachs Report Reveals US Construction Productivity Decline: Innovation and Regulation to Blame
summaries.blurb: Goldman Sachs' latest report reveals a troubling trend in the US construction industry, highlighting a dramatic decline in productivity that has averaged 0.6% per year since 1965. Economist Elsie Peng attributes this stagnation to stagnant innovation, rising regulatory pressures, and mismeasurement of output, raising questions about the sector's ability to adapt and thrive in a rapidly changing economy. As the construction landscape evolves, the report emphasizes the urgent need for transformation to unlock potential productivity gains.

summaries.title: Why Record-High Copper Prices Aren’t Forecast to Last
summaries.summaryText:
A January report from Goldman Sachs discusses the recent surge in copper prices and forecasts a decline for 2026. Copper prices on the London Metals Exchange rose 22%, reaching a record high of $13,387 per tonne in early January. Goldman Sachs predicts that while prices may hold near $13,000 in Q1 2026, they could drop to $11,000 per tonne by year-end.

One primary factor influencing copper prices is the anticipated announcement of refined copper tariffs from the US administration, which has led to increased stockpiling by buyers in the US. Analyst Eoin Dinsmore notes that this stockpiling is creating short-term scarcity outside of the US. The report identifies three key drivers for the price increase: heightened demand in December, expectations of AI-related demand for data centers, and favorable US economic policymaking that has supported asset prices.

Uncertainty over the tariff decision is currently propping up prices. A potential 15% tariff announcement by mid-2026 could signify the end of US stockpiling and a subsequent price drop. However, if the announcement is delayed until 2027, prices might fall further as the market shifts focus to supply issues. 

Goldman Sachs also notes a substantial global copper surplus, estimating a surplus of 600 kilotonnes in 2025 and increasing their surplus forecast for 2026 to 300 kilotonnes. Weakness in China's demand for refined copper and adjustments to US stockpiling figures further underscore the expected market dynamics. The report concludes that copper’s fair price is approximately $11,500 per tonne, indicating the current high prices may be unsustainable.

Source URL: https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/why-record-high-copper-prices-arent-forecast-to-last
summaries.headline: Goldman Sachs Predicts Copper Prices to Plummet from Record Highs as Market Dynamics Shift in 2026
summaries.blurb: Goldman Sachs' latest report reveals that while copper prices soared to a record $13,387 per tonne, a dramatic decline is on the horizon for 2026. As US stockpiling and tariff uncertainty create a temporary scarcity, analysts predict prices could plummet to $11,000 by year-end, driven by a looming global surplus and decreasing demand from China. With market dynamics shifting, the high prices we've seen may not hold for long.

summaries.title: US GDP Growth Is Projected to Outperform Economist Forecasts in 2026
summaries.summaryText:
A January report from Goldman Sachs projects stronger US GDP growth in 2026 than many economists expect. According to David Mericle, chief US economist, the firm forecasts a 2.5% year-over-year GDP growth rate for the fourth quarter, above the consensus estimate of 2.1%. For the entire year, GDP is expected to grow 2.8%, with the probability of a recession falling from 30% to 20%.

Key drivers include the impact of tax cuts from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which may enhance consumer and business spending. Mericle highlights that productivity growth, bolstered by advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), will be a significant contributor to economic expansion moving forward.

In terms of inflation, core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation is estimated to drop to 2.1% by December, while core CPI is expected at 2%. These forecasts are lower than the consensus estimates. Mericle notes that past inflation pressures, particularly from tariffs, are dissipating, leading to a more favorable inflation outlook.

For the labor market, Goldman Sachs expects the unemployment rate to stabilize at 4.5% but indicates several risks, including reduced job growth due to AI and a narrower job market. Despite these challenges, there are signs of stabilization in recent employment reports, which may lead to improved hiring.

Regarding Federal Reserve policies, Goldman Sachs anticipates two rate cuts in 2026, with the fed funds rate poised to end the cycle between 3%-3.25%. This adjustment is anticipated due to lower inflation, which may ease some disagreements among Fed officials regarding the terminal rate.

Source URL: https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/us-gdp-growth-is-projected-to-outperform-economist-forecasts-in-2026
summaries.headline: Goldman Sachs Forecasts Stronger-than-Expected US GDP Growth in 2026, Citing Tax Cuts and AI Advancements
summaries.blurb: Goldman Sachs projects a surprising surge in US GDP growth for 2026, forecasting a year-over-year increase of 2.8%, driven by tax cuts and advancements in artificial intelligence. Chief US economist David Mericle highlights a reduced recession risk and a brighter inflation outlook, with core PCE expected to decline to 2.1%. As the economy shifts, the labor market faces challenges, yet signs of stabilization offer a hopeful outlook for hiring.

summaries.title: Productivity Stagnation in the Construction Industry: An International Perspective
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from Goldman Sachs titled "Productivity Stagnation in the Construction Industry: An International Perspective" highlights the significant decline in productivity within the US construction sector from 1970 to 2024. The report reveals that productivity in this industry has decreased by 30%, contrasting sharply with the overall economy, where productivity has more than doubled during the same period.

The report examines various factors contributing to this productivity stagnation. It discusses traditional work practices, fragmentation within the industry, and challenges related to labor force skills. The findings indicate that the adoption of modern technologies and innovative practices has been slower in construction compared to other sectors.

Another critical perspective offered in the report is the international comparison, indicating that US construction productivity lags behind that of several other countries. The report provides data illustrating these disparities and emphasizes the need for improvements in operational efficiency to close this gap. Notably, the document outlines potential strategies for enhancing productivity, such as better project management, investment in technology, and workforce training.

Overall, the report provides a comprehensive analysis of the challenges facing the US construction industry, illustrating the need for a concerted effort to improve productivity levels.

Source URL: https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/goldman-sachs-research/productivity-stagnation-in-construction-industry
summaries.headline: US Construction Productivity Lags Behind as Industry Faces Stagnation Challenges, Says Goldman Sachs Report
summaries.blurb: In a revealing February report, Goldman Sachs uncovers a troubling 30% decline in productivity within the US construction industry since 1970—starkly contrasted by a doubling of productivity in the broader economy. Highlighting traditional practices and skills gaps, the report underscores the urgent need for modernization and offers strategies such as innovative technologies and improved project management to help bridge the international productivity gap. With a call for comprehensive reform, this analysis poses critical questions for the future of construction in America.

summaries.title: Dodge Momentum Index Declines 7% in February
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Dodge Construction Network reveals that the Dodge Momentum Index (DMI) declined by 7.3% in February, reaching 250.0, down from a downwardly revised January figure of 269.8. Commercial planning saw an 8.9% drop, while institutional planning slowed by 4.0%. According to Sarah Martin, Associate Director of Forecasting at Dodge Construction Network, “Planning momentum continued to normalize in February after a surge in activity in the back half of 2025.” 

The report notes that risks related to costs, labor, and geopolitics are likely to hinder builder confidence in the short term, although a robust planning pipeline points to potential construction spending acceleration in 2027. In the commercial sector, planning momentum decreased across all sectors except for warehouses. All institutional sectors also experienced slowdowns, with public buildings facing significant contraction. Nevertheless, areas such as retail stores, recreational buildings, data centers, and healthcare facilities displayed elevated project momentum.

Compared to February 2025, the DMI increased by 18.7%. The commercial segment rose by 12.3% (4.4% growth excluding data centers), and the institutional segment surged by 34.0% year-over-year. In February, 23 projects valued at $100 million or more commenced planning, including notable commercial projects like the $500 million CyrusOne Data Center in Whitney, Texas, and the $448 million TX12 Data Center in San Antonio, Texas. Major institutional projects included the $400 million Orange County Convention Center Grand Concourse expansion in Orlando, Florida, and a $254 million school replacement project in Upper Marlboro, Maryland. 

The DMI serves as a monthly indicator based on a three-month moving value of nonresidential building projects in planning, which typically leads nonresidential construction spending by approximately one to 18 months. 

Source URL: https://www.construction.com/dodge-momentum-index/dodge-momentum-index-declines-7-in-february/
summaries.headline: Dodge Momentum Index Plummets 7.3% in February Amid Cost and Labor Concerns
summaries.blurb: The Dodge Momentum Index (DMI) experienced a significant 7.3% decline in February, highlighting ongoing concerns in both cost and labor that are impacting builder confidence. Despite this dip, the long-term outlook remains promising, with a robust planning pipeline indicating a potential acceleration in construction spending by 2027. Notable commercial projects, including two massive data centers in Texas and a major convention center expansion in Florida, illustrate pockets of growth amid the slowdown.

summaries.title: Construction Starts Grow 1% in January
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from Dodge Construction Network highlights that total construction starts increased by 0.7% in January 2026 to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $1.24 trillion. Nonresidential building starts declined by 15.4%, residential starts fell by 6.4%, while nonbuilding starts surged by 24.3%. Year-over-year, total construction starts rose by 5.0%, despite nonresidential starts down by 10.3% and residential starts down by 17.0%. 

In the residential sector, construction starts fell to an annual rate of $345 billion, with single-family starts increasing by 1.5% month-over-month, while multifamily starts decreased by 17.8%. Compared to January 2025, residential starts were down 17.0%. The largest multifamily projects started include the $335 million 38 Gramercy Park East Condominiums in New York.

For nonresidential building, construction starts dropped to $378 billion. While commercial starts plummeted by 27.3%, certain areas like warehouses and retail saw increases. It was noted that the manufacturing sector experienced significant growth, up by 97.5% in January. 

In the nonbuilding category, the $522 billion rate was heavily influenced by a dramatic increase of 184.8% in electric power/utilities. Key projects included the $12 billion Port Arthur LNG project in Texas.

Regionally, construction starts increased in the Northeast, South Central, and South Atlantic, while they declined in the West and Midwest. 

Source URL: https://www.construction.com/company-news/construction-starts-grow-1-in-january-2/
summaries.headline: Construction Starts Up 0.7% in January Amid Mixed Sector Performance
summaries.blurb: In January 2026, total construction starts saw a modest increase of 0.7%, reaching a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $1.24 trillion, according to the latest report from Dodge Construction Network. While nonresidential and residential sectors faced declines, a remarkable surge in nonbuilding projects—particularly a staggering 184.8% rise in electric power and utilities—signals shifting dynamics in the industry. Key projects, including the $12 billion Port Arthur LNG facility, highlight the sector's resilience amidst mixed performance.

summaries.title: Dodge Momentum Index Declines 6% in January
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from Dodge Construction Network reveals that the Dodge Momentum Index (DMI) declined 6.3% in January to 272.7 (2000=100) from a revised December reading of 291.0. In January, commercial planning decreased by 7.2%, while institutional planning dropped by 4.4%. Sarah Martin, Associate Director of Forecasting at Dodge Construction Network, noted that “planning momentum cooled in January across most commercial and institutional sectors.” Data center projects are mentioned as a strong support for planning levels, although there is a transition to a more sustainable growth pattern following high activity in late 2025.

On the commercial side, all sectors experienced slowdown except for retail stores. In the institutional sector, January witnessed reductions in planning for education, healthcare, and public buildings, while recreational and religious projects saw growth. Year-over-year, the DMI was up 29% compared to January 2025, with the commercial segment rising by 26% (17% when excluding data centers) and the institutional segment increasing by 34%.

In total, 35 projects with a value of $100 million or more were planned in January. Notable commercial projects included the $500 million IEP Data Center in Pennsylvania, the $400 million Mountain Road Technology Park Data Center in Virginia, and the $350 million Bitfarm Data Center in Pennsylvania. Significant institutional projects included the $250 million USACE Barracks in Fort Hood, Texas, the $175 million UEPH Barracks in Virginia, and the $148 million Eurofins Lancaster Biopharmaceutical Laboratory in Pennsylvania.

The DMI serves as a monthly indicator, based on a three-month moving value of nonresidential building projects entering planning, which influences nonresidential construction spending forecasts by 12 to 18 months. 

Source URL: https://www.construction.com/company-news/dodge-momentum-index-declines-6-in-january/
summaries.headline: Dodge Momentum Index Drops 6.3% in January, Highlighting Slowdown in Commercial and Institutional Planning
summaries.blurb: The Dodge Momentum Index (DMI) saw a notable decline of 6.3% in January, signaling a slowdown in commercial and institutional planning. Despite a dip across most sectors, data center projects continue to lend support, hinting at a shift toward more sustainable growth after the activity surge of late 2025. With various large-scale projects still on the horizon, the report provides a nuanced view of the evolving landscape in nonresidential construction.

summaries.title: ABC: Construction Hiring Remained Slow in January
summaries.summaryText:
A March 13 report from Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) outlines hiring trends in the construction industry for January. It states that there were 231,000 job openings at the end of January, based on data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). A job opening is defined as any unfilled position for which employers are actively recruiting. The number of job openings in the construction sector decreased by 14,000 from December and is down by 1,000 compared to January of the previous year.

ABC Chief Economist Anirban Basu noted that while construction hiring accelerated, reaching its fastest rate since the first half of 2025, this increase is still relatively modest. Basu stated, “The industry’s hiring rate is still slower than at any point between the start of the data series in 2001 and the end of 2019.” He also highlighted that contractors maintain a positive outlook, as reflected in ABC’s Construction Confidence Index, which indicates that they believe staffing levels will increase over the next six months. However, this confidence has persisted over the years even as the hiring pace has remained lackluster.

Source URL: https://www.abc.org/News-Media/News-Releases/abc-construction-hiring-remained-slow-in-january
summaries.headline: Construction Job Openings Dip to 231,000 Despite Hiring Optimism in January
summaries.blurb: In a recent report from Associated Builders and Contractors, job openings in the construction sector dipped to 231,000 in January, highlighting a modest hiring trend despite ongoing optimism among contractors. While the hiring rate has quickened since early 2025, experts warn it still lags behind pre-2020 levels. As optimism about future staffing increases persists, the industry faces a challenging balancing act between confidence and actual recruitment rates.

summaries.title: Industrial MSA Deep Dive: Near-Full Occupancy & Minimal CMBS Delinquency
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Trepp discusses the robust performance of the industrial real estate sector in the United States, highlighting minimal delinquency rates and high occupancy levels as of February 2026. 

Occupancy rates for industrial properties in the top 25 metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) are notably strong, with Charlotte, Pittsburgh, and St. Louis reporting 100% occupancy. Other significant markets such as Riverside-San Bernardino, Phoenix, New York, and San Francisco maintain occupancy rates between approximately 98.5% and 99.8%, resulting in an average occupancy rate above 92% across these MSAs.

Delinquency rates for industrial loans are exceptionally low, with a weighted average of just 0.37%. The highest delinquency in the top 25 MSAs is seen in Chicago at 2.45%, while other notable rates include Boston at 1.73% and Tampa at 1.24%. Many metropolitan areas report nearly zero delinquent industrial loans, indicating strong loan performance in this sector compared to multifamily delinquency rates, which are closer to 50-60 basis points.

Capital markets activity reflects these positive fundamentals, with approximately $3.8 billion in industrial loan originations in the fourth quarter of 2025. Riverside-San Bernardino led the origination activity, followed by Atlanta, New York, Los Angeles, and Dallas-Fort Worth. The transactions are characterized by significant portfolio deals usually driven by institutional investors seeking operational efficiencies.

The overall conclusion is that the industrial real estate sector remains one of the most stable within the commercial real estate market, demonstrating solid occupancy, minimal delinquency, and continued capital inflow.

Source URL: https://www.trepp.com/trepptalk/industrial-msa-deep-dive
summaries.headline: Industrial Real Estate Thrives with Near-Perfect Occupancy and Record Low Delinquency Rates
summaries.blurb: A recent Trepp report reveals that the industrial real estate sector is thriving, marked by nearly full occupancy and strikingly low delinquency rates as of February 2026. With top markets like Charlotte and Pittsburgh boasting 100% occupancy, the sector showcases an impressive average occupancy exceeding 92%. This stability fuels strong capital market activity, positioning industrial real estate as one of the most resilient segments in the commercial landscape.

summaries.title: Americas First
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from Goldman Sachs outlines the Trump Administration's efforts to establish a more assertive foreign policy at the start of 2026, centering around a new initiative termed the “Donroe Doctrine.” This doctrine is positioned as an extension of the Monroe Doctrine, with the goal of enhancing U.S. influence and control throughout the Western Hemisphere. 

The document discusses the potential impacts of this policy shift, indicating that the evolution from “America First” to “Americas First” could have significant implications for various aspects, including economic conditions, asset valuations, and geopolitical risks. Specifics on the anticipated changes to bilateral relations and foreign economic policies are explored, although the report does not provide in-depth analysis or implications of these shifts.

Furthermore, the document signals an urgency for stakeholders to understand how this new direction in U.S. foreign policy may affect both regional dynamics and global economic systems as it unfolds. The reference to a “more forceful foreign policy” suggests a clear posture aimed at repositioning U.S. interests in a manner that may lead to increased engagement or confrontation with other nations within the hemisphere.

Ultimately, the report serves to alert readers to the potential ramifications of the “Donroe Doctrine” and the broader concept of “Americas First” as a framework guiding U.S. strategy and foreign relations moving forward. 

Source URL: https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/top-of-mind/americas-first
summaries.headline: Goldman Sachs Highlights Shift to "Americas First" with New "Donroe Doctrine" Initiative Under Trump Administration
summaries.blurb: In a groundbreaking report, Goldman Sachs unveils the Trump Administration's new “Donroe Doctrine,” a bold shift toward an assertive foreign policy dubbed “Americas First.” This initiative aims to bolster U.S. influence in the Western Hemisphere and outlines significant implications for economic conditions, asset valuations, and geopolitical dynamics. Stakeholders are urged to closely monitor how this evolving directive could reshape regional and global interactions.

summaries.title: Construction Employment Falls By 11,000 In February With Declines In Residential And Nonresidential As Firms Worry About Demand Levels
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from the Associated General Contractors of America reveals that construction employment fell by 11,000 jobs in February, encompassing both residential and nonresidential sectors. This decline comes on the heels of stronger hiring in January, which had been reported more favorably than initially understood. The current downturn indicates that contractors are adopting a more cautious stance regarding workforce expansion, primarily due to uncertainties related to material prices and project demand.

Macrina Wilkins, the association’s director of market insights, stated, “Contractors may be more reluctant to add workers amid uncertainty about how much they will pay for construction materials and demand for certain types of construction projects.” Despite this monthly drop, the construction employment sector has experienced growth at a faster pace compared to the broader economy over the past year, underscoring the sector's resilience even in the face of current challenges.

The report emphasizes that both residential and nonresidential construction areas have seen job losses, reflecting a broader trend of caution among firms as they reassess their hiring strategies in light of prevailing economic conditions. The overall employment picture within the construction industry remains a point of discussion as firms grapple with these evolving challenges.

Source URL: https://news.agc.org/economics/construction-employment-falls-by-11000-in-february-with-declines-in-residential-and-nonresidential-as-firms-worry-about-demand-levels/
summaries.headline: Construction Employment Dips by 11,000 as Firms Cautiously Navigate Economic Uncertainties
summaries.blurb: A recent report from the Associated General Contractors of America reveals a dip in construction employment, with 11,000 jobs lost in February across both residential and nonresidential sectors. This cautious trend, following a surge in hiring the previous month, highlights contractors' growing concerns about fluctuating material costs and demand for projects. Despite this setback, the construction industry continues to outpace the broader economy in job growth over the past year, showcasing its resilience amid uncertainty.

summaries.title: Extreme Increases In Aluminum, Steel And Copper Costs Drive Up Prices For Construction Materials In January; Spending Ends 2025 Down From 2024
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from AGC Construction Data highlights significant cost increases in construction materials, with the producer price index for materials and services used in nonresidential construction rising by 2.9 percent from January 2025 to February 2026. The report also notes a decline in construction spending, which fell by 0.4 percent from December 2024 to December 2025. This analysis was conducted by the Associated General Contractors of America based on two government reports released on the same date.

The association's officials attribute the rising costs to tariffs on key materials, which they argue inflate prices. They are calling on federal officials to promptly renew vital infrastructure legislation, such as the surface transportation bill, to provide stability for domestic suppliers, which in turn may lead to increased production.

Ken Simonson, the association’s chief economist, stated, “Although producer indexes are based on selling prices of domestic producers, the steep tariffs on imported metals and products are clearly enabling U.S. sellers to push up costs for construction materials and equipment.” Simonson emphasized that ensuring domestic producers have greater certainty regarding future demand could incentivize them to enhance production capacities, potentially resulting in lower prices for construction materials in the long term.

Overall, the findings underline economic pressures within the construction sector, particularly regarding material costs and spending trends, while also highlighting the influence of policy decisions on production and pricing.

Source URL: https://news.agc.org/economics/extreme-increases-in-aluminum-steel-and-copper-costs-drive-up-prices-for-construction-materials-in-january-spending-ends-2025-down-from-2024/
summaries.headline: Construction Material Costs Surge Amid Declining Spending, Tariff Pressures Highlighted in February Report
summaries.blurb: A new report from AGC Construction Data reveals a concerning 2.9 percent spike in construction material costs, driven largely by tariffs on essential metals like aluminum, steel, and copper. While construction spending has dipped slightly, industry leaders stress the urgency for renewed infrastructure legislation to stabilize prices and boost domestic production. This dynamic landscape underscores the critical link between policy decisions and economic pressures facing the construction sector.
